content: Teething is the developmental process in which an infant's teeth begin to emerge sequentially through the gums. This process can start as early as three months of age or as late as twelve months in some cases. Rarely, a baby may be born with one or more teeth already present. Typically, the emergence of teeth begins between six and nine months of age, and it can take several years for all 20 primary teeth, also known as deciduous, baby, or milk teeth, to fully erupt. The term cutting teeth is often used to describe this process. The eruption of teeth generally occurs in pairs. For example, one upper central incisor will emerge, followed by the other upper central incisor, before the next set of teeth begins to appear. The usual sequence of tooth eruption is as follows: 1. Lower central incisors (2 teeth) 2. Upper central incisors (2 teeth) 3. Upper lateral incisors (2 teeth) 4. Lower lateral incisors (2 teeth) 5. First molars (4 teeth) 6. Canines (4 teeth) 7. Second molars (4 teeth) In general, female infants tend to experience tooth eruption earlier than male infants. The timing and pattern of teething are largely influenced by genetic factors. Importantly, the timing of tooth eruption has no correlation with the overall health of the child. During teething, the teeth push through the gum tissue, which can cause various symptoms. Common signs of teething include: Irritability or a poor mood Decreased appetite A tendency to chew on objects Swelling or bruising of the gums Increased salivation A runny nose It is important to note that teething does not cause fever. While a slight increase in body temperature may occur as the teeth break through the gums, this is not sufficient to make the infant ill. Infants often chew on objects to alleviate discomfort associated with teething. However, this behavior can pose a choking hazard if the objects are small enough to be swallowed or if they break apart during chewing. For this reason, teething rings and toys are specifically designed with safe textures to provide relief during this stage. If an infant appears to be in significant pain, some healthcare providers may recommend the use of anti-inflammatory medications or child-safe pain relief products containing benzocaine. Additionally, some infants find relief by chewing on cold objects, such as chilled teething rings. Dental professionals advise parents to begin brushing an infant's teeth as soon as they emerge. It is not recommended to wait until the teething process is complete to establish good oral hygiene practices. However, dentists often advise against the use of fluoride toothpaste during the teething stage.
